items.title: EMVCo merchant QR
items.description: Build and parse EMVCo merchant QR payloads (the NepalPay and Fonepay scan-to-pay format): TLV, CRC-16 check, bigint amounts, clear errors.
items.summary: Pure helpers for EMVCo merchant-presented QR payloads, the format behind NepalPay QR, Fonepay and most national QR schemes. `buildMerchantQr` turns typed fields into a payload with its CRC; `parseMerchantQr` checks a scanned one (structure, CRC, payload format, mandatory objects) and returns the fields, or an error code and a sentence to show. Amounts are bigint minor units. No React, no browser globals, no dependency.
use: A "receive money" or shop counter screen: build the payload on your server (or in the browser for a preview) and draw it with `QrCode` or `PaymentQrCard`.
A scanner screen: `parseMerchantQr` on the decoded text, then show the merchant and amount for the person to confirm.
`verifyMerchantQrCrc` to reject a damaged or edited code before you read it.
avoid: Inventing a merchant account template. The GUID and sub-fields (ids 26 to 51) come from your acquirer or switch; this module only lays them out.
Trusting a parsed payload as a real merchant. A payload that parses is well formed; the payment network decides whether the merchant exists.

exports.name: parseMerchantQr
exports.description:
Parses and checks a scanned payload. Never throws: a bad payload comes back as `{ ok: false, code, message }` so a
scanner screen can say what went wrong. Checks the structure, the CRC, the payload format ('01') and the mandatory
objects (a merchant account, 52, 53, 58, 59, 60).

exports.description: True when the payload ends with a CRC object whose value matches the text before it (case-insensitive hex).

items.title: QrCode
items.description: A dependency-free QR code in one SVG path: byte mode, versions 1 to 40, four error correction levels. Dark on light in both themes; renders on the server.
items.summary: Draws text as a QR code. The encoder (`encodeQr`, also on `@punji/ui/qr-code/matrix`) implements ISO/IEC 18004 byte mode for versions 1 to 40 and levels L, M, Q and H, chooses the smallest version and the best mask, and raises the error correction when there is room. The component draws the grid as one SVG path with a 4-module quiet zone, dark on light in both themes, because many scanners cannot read an inverted code. It uses no hooks, so it renders on the server.
use: A payment code (with `PaymentQrCard` for the full screen), a link to an app, a receipt reference.
`qrSvgPath` to draw the same grid in a canvas, a PDF or a server-rendered image.
avoid: Light modules on a dark background. Keep `foreground` dark and `background` light.
Text that only the code carries: write the merchant and amount beside it too.

items.title: PaymentQrCard

items.summary: The "scan to pay" card for a shop counter or a "receive money" screen. With `onAmountChange`, a static code gets an "Add amount" fallback; you build the new payload and pass it back.

`renderQr` to draw the code with your own renderer or a server image; `actions` for share and download.
avoid: Building the payload from the props you also display: build it once (`buildMerchantQr` or your server) and pass only the payload.
Treating the shown amount as authoritative. The payer's app reads the payload; your server confirms the payment.

items.title: AmountKeypad
items.description: An on-screen amount keypad for wallets: exact decimal entry in paisa, lakh and crore grouping, quick amounts, a max that refuses keys and says why.
items.summary: An on-screen number pad for send money, pay at a shop and top-up screens. It builds an exact ASCII decimal string at the currency's minor-unit digits and reports the amount as bigint minor units. The figure is large and grouped in lakh and crore for NPR. A key that would pass `max`, add a third decimal or overflow is refused, and the reason is announced. Quick amounts set the whole figure. It does not check a balance or a fee.

`max` from your server: the balance or the per-transaction limit.
`quickAmounts` for top-ups (Rs 100, 200, 500) and tips.
avoid: Desktop forms: use `CurrencyInput`, which works with any keyboard.
Treating `max` as the check. The server checks the amount, the balance and the limit again.

items.description: A transaction PIN pad that never writes the digits to the page: dots, a spoken count, an optional crypto-random key order and a fingerprint slot.
items.summary: An on-screen pad for a transaction PIN (MPIN). Each digit shows as a filled dot; the digits themselves are never written to the page, not as text, a value or a hidden input, and the Tab stop never moves to the last key pressed. A screen reader hears "2 of 4 digits entered". `shuffle` draws a random key order with `crypto.getRandomValues`, against shoulder surfing and smudges; change `shuffleKey` to draw again. `onComplete` fires once with the full PIN.

`extraKey` for a fingerprint or face button in the empty bottom-left cell.
`shuffle` with `shuffleKey={attempt}` after a wrong PIN.
avoid: Login passwords or codes sent by SMS: use `OtpInput`, which supports autofill.
Checking the PIN in the browser. Send it to your server, clear the value and show the result.

points: The PIN lives in your state. Keep it in memory only, send it over TLS, clear it after the request, and never log it.

items.enforcementNote: UI is not enforcement. This component is a UX safeguard. It does not enforce anything. Authorisation, step-up authentication, limits, payee checks, session expiry and validation must be enforced on the server. Hidden or disabled controls are not access control.

items.title: MobileNumberInput
items.description: A Nepal mobile number field: +977 prefix, pasted country codes and Devanagari digits, 984-1234567 grouping and NTC, Ncell or SmartCell detection.
items.summary: A field for a Nepal mobile number. It shows +977 as a fixed prefix, accepts a pasted +977 or 00977 number, spaces, dashes and Devanagari digits, groups the digits as 984-1234567 and names the operator (NTC, Ncell, SmartCell) from the first three digits. `onValueChange` gives the state, the national digits, the E.164 form and the operator. The prefix table is data in `@punji/ui/nepal/mobile`, so a new range is a prop, not a release.

Wallet sign-up and "send to mobile".
`parseNepalMobile` and `formatNepalMobile` on the server for the same rules.
avoid: Proving a number exists or who owns it: send an OTP.
Landlines and other countries: this is Nepal mobile only.

exports.name: MobileOperator
exports.description:
Nepal mobile numbers: normalise what was typed or pasted (+977, 00977, spaces, dashes, Devanagari digits), check
the shape (ten digits starting with 9) and detect the operator from the three-digit prefix. The prefix table is
data: pass your own `operators` when the regulator assigns a new range, without waiting for a release.

A valid shape is not a reachable number, and the prefix shows the operator the range was issued to: a number moved
with mobile number portability, if Nepal adopts it, keeps its old prefix. Confirm with the operator or your
top-up aggregator before you charge.

The operator is announced in a polite live region ("Operator: Ncell"); the visible badge is hidden from screen readers to avoid reading it twice.

notes.title: Limits
points: The prefix shows which operator the range was issued to. A ported number, if Nepal adopts number portability, keeps its old prefix; confirm with your top-up aggregator.
The default table: NTC 984, 985, 986, 974, 975, 976; Ncell 980, 981, 982, 970; SmartCell 961, 962, 988. Pass `operators` to change it.

items.title: TransferReview
items.description: The last screen before money moves: amount in figures and words, a spoofing-checked recipient name, changed fields marked, fee and exact total.
items.summary: The confirm step of a transfer. `ConfirmAmount` reads the amount back in figures and in words, because a slipped zero is hard to miss in words. The recipient name is shown inside `<bdi>` with bidi controls and invisible characters removed, and checked with `detectSpoofing`: mixed scripts, look-alike letters, or a look-alike of a payee the person already trusts. A risky name blocks the confirm button until the person ticks that they checked it. Rows that changed since the person last saw them say "Changed (was …)" in words, not only in colour. Display only: it computes the total (amount + fee, exact bigint) and nothing else.
use: Every transfer, bill payment and wallet send, as the step before the PIN or the hold-to-confirm.
`knownPayees` with the person's saved payees, so "Paypa1" next to a saved "Paypal" is caught.
`previousAmount` and `details[].previous` after an edit, so the person sees what is different.
`confirm` with `HoldToConfirm` for large amounts; `verification` with `PayeeVerification`.
avoid: Treating the name check as payee verification. It looks at the text only; your bank or scheme confirms who holds the account.
Rounded or compact amounts here. Show every digit: this is the figure the person agrees to.

notes.title: Security boundary
points: The name check catches the tricks seen on payee names (look-alike Cyrillic and Greek letters, bidi overrides, invisible characters, look-alikes of trusted names). It cannot prove a name is safe.

items.title: PayeeVerification
items.description: Show a Confirmation of Payee or Verification of Payee result: match, close match with the real name, no match with an acknowledgement, or unavailable.
items.summary: Displays the answer your server got from a payee name check (UK Confirmation of Payee, the EU Verification of Payee required since October 2025, or your bank's own lookup). A match is quiet. A close match shows the name the bank holds and offers to use it. No match says plainly that the money may go to someone else, and continuing needs an explicit acknowledgement. Unavailable says the name could not be checked, which is not a match. Names render inside `<bdi>`, cleaned and checked for spoofing.

items.title: HoldToConfirm
items.description: Friction for high-risk actions: press and hold (pointer or held Space/Enter) to confirm, or a cooling-off countdown before the button works.
items.summary: Two kinds of deliberate friction. In `hold` mode the action runs only after the button is held for `holdMs`; letting go early cancels and says so. Holding Space or Enter works the same, and key repeat is ignored. In `cooling-off` mode the button is unavailable for `delaySeconds` after it appears, with the time left in its label, giving a rushed or coached person a moment to stop. It is a real `<button>`; progress is announced at the start and end, not every frame.
use: Large or unusual transfers, adding a payee, closing an account, cancelling a fixed deposit early.
`cooling-off` after a scam warning, or when a risk score is high.
avoid: Everyday actions: friction everywhere teaches people to push through it.
Hold as the only way to do something essential for people who cannot hold a press; offer cooling-off or a second confirm instead.

items.title: SessionTimeoutWarning
items.description: The sign-out warning WCAG 2.2.1 asks for: at least 20 seconds notice, one action to stay, a visible countdown announced only at key moments.
items.summary: An alert dialog that opens `warnBefore` milliseconds (at least 20 seconds, per WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable) before the session in `expiresAt` ends. The countdown is visible every second but announced only when it opens and at one minute, 30 and 10 seconds. Focus goes to "Stay signed in" and returns afterwards; Tab stays inside; Esc also stays signed in. When time runs out `onExpire` is called once and "You have been signed out" is announced.

items.title: SecureField
items.description: Inputs for passwords, one-time codes, PINs, card data and account numbers with the right autocomplete, no spellcheck and no value in the DOM.
items.summary: A field for secrets with the browser attributes set per `kind`: `current-password`, `new-password`, `one-time-code` (SMS autofill), `pin`, `cc-number`, `cc-csc`, `cc-exp`, `account-number` and `secret-answer`. Spellcheck, autocorrect and autocapitalise are off, so the text is not sent to a cloud dictionary. The value is pushed into the input's property, never its `value` attribute (React writes that for controlled inputs, and CSS attribute selectors can read it out), nor into a data attribute, title or label. `secureFieldAttributes(kind)` when you render the input yourself.

items.title: Spoofing detection
items.description: detectSpoofing checks a payee name for mixed scripts, look-alike letters, bidi controls and invisible characters, after Unicode UTS #39.
items.summary: Pure helpers after Unicode UTS #39. `detectSpoofing(name, { known })` returns a risk (none, review, high), the issues with a sentence each, the scripts used, a cleaned `display` string and the skeleton. It flags bidi overrides and isolates, invisible characters (keeping the joiners Devanagari, Bengali and Persian need), controls, Latin mixed with look-alike Cyrillic, Greek, Armenian or Cherokee letters, names written entirely in look-alikes, compatibility forms, stacked marks and odd spaces, and any name that looks like one in `known` without being it. `skeleton` and `areConfusable` compare two names.
use: Payee names, merchant names, account nicknames and anything else a person will trust because of how it looks.
`known` with saved payees and the verified account name.
avoid: Using `risk: none` as proof a name is genuine. It finds tricks; it does not verify identity.
Rejecting every non-Latin name: single-script names in any script pass.

exports.name: detectSpoofing
exports.description:
Checks a payee or account name for the tricks used to make one name pass for another. Returns the risk, the
issues with a sentence each, the scripts, a cleaned `display` string and the skeleton. Pass `known` (saved payees,
the bank's verified name) to catch a look-alike of a name the person trusts.

```ts
detectSpoofing('PаyPal').risk;                       // 'high': Cyrillic "а" among Latin letters
detectSpoofing('Ram Bahadur Thapa').risk;            // 'none'
detectSpoofing('Paypa1', { known: ['Paypal'] }).lookalikeOf; // 'Paypal'
```

exports.name: skeleton
exports.description:
The comparison skeleton: NFKC (full-width and mathematical letters fold), hidden characters removed, look-alikes
mapped to the Latin letter they imitate, lowercased, "rn" read as "m", spaces collapsed.
`skeleton('PаyPaI')` and `skeleton('paypal')` are both 'paypal'.

exports.name: areConfusable
exports.description: True when two different names look the same (equal skeletons, different text).

props.description: The UTS #39-style skeleton used for comparison. Two names with the same skeleton look alike.

exports.name: SpoofIssueKind
exports.description:
Name spoofing checks for money movement: before someone sends money to "PayPal", is it really Latin "PayPal" or
"PаyPal" with a Cyrillic "а"? Pure and dependency-free, after Unicode UTS #39 (security mechanisms): mixed-script
detection with the "highly restrictive" allowances (Latin with Han and Japanese kana, Han with Bopomofo, Han with
Hangul), a skeleton for confusable comparison, and checks for bidi controls, invisible characters, controls,
compatibility forms and stacked marks. The confusable table is a focused subset (Cyrillic, Greek, Armenian and
Latin look-alikes of Latin letters and digits), not the full Unicode confusables.txt: it catches the attacks seen on
payee names, it does not prove a name is safe. Your server still verifies the payee.

props.description: Names the person already trusts (saved payees, the verified account name). A different name that looks the same is flagged 'high'.

notes.title: Limits
points: The confusable table is a focused subset (Cyrillic, Greek, Armenian, Cherokee and Latin look-alikes of Latin letters and digits), not the full confusables.txt, to stay under 3 kB.
Mixed-script rules follow the UTS #39 "highly restrictive" allowances: Latin with Han and kana, Han with Bopomofo, Han with Hangul.
Names longer than 512 characters are checked on their first 512.

items.title: Global money
items.description: Exact money for any currency and locale: lakh/crore or western grouping, 0 to 3 decimals, 18 digit scripts, exact compact notation and ISO 4217 data.
items.summary: The money formatter is currency-generic: the exponent comes from Intl (JPY 0, USD 2, KWD 3) or `exponent` when your ledger follows ISO 4217 where CLDR differs. Grouping follows the locale, so en-IN and bn-BD print 12,34,567; `grouping: 'south-asian'` forces lakh and crore on any locale (common for PKR) and switches compact notation to L and Cr. Input accepts digits of 18 scripts (Devanagari, Bengali, Arabic-Indic, Persian, Thai, Gujarati, Tamil and more), and `toScriptDigits` prints them. Compact notation rounds once, from the exact decimal string, never through a float. ISO 4217 codes, numeric codes and minor units load from their own subpath.
use: Any currency screen: `createMoneyFormatter({ currency, locale })` once per table.
`grouping` and `exponent` when local practice differs from CLDR.
`@punji/ui/money/iso4217` for a currency picker or numeric codes from a payment message.
`currencyAmountInWords` for cheques and read-back lines in English.
avoid: Compact figures for anything stored or summed: they are display-rounded.
Assuming every currency has two decimals.

exports.description:
ISO 4217 active currency data: alphabetic code, numeric code and minor units (the number of decimals), for the
currencies in circulation (List One, amendments through 2026: ZWG replaced ZWL, XCG replaced ANG, SLE replaced
SLL, and BGN went with Bulgaria's move to the euro on 1 January 2026). Funds, precious metals and testing codes
(XAU, XDR, XTS, BOV, CLF...) are left out. A separate subpath, `@punji/ui/money/iso4217`, so the ~1.5 kB of data
loads only where a page needs it (a dynamic import of that subpath).

Minor units here are ISO's. Intl (CLDR) disagrees for a few currencies where the smallest coin is out of use
(ISO IQD 3, CLDR 0); pass `exponent: isoMinorUnits(code)` to `createMoneyFormatter` when your ledger uses ISO's.

props.description: Word after the amount. Default 'only' or 'मात्र'. Pass '' for none.

props.name: unitPosition
props.description: Where the major-unit word goes: 'before' ("Rupees one hundred") or 'after' ("one hundred rupees"). Default 'before' in English, 'after' in Nepali.

examples.title: South Asia and the Gulf
examples.note: INR, BDT in Bengali digits, PKR with lakh grouping forced, LKR, and KWD with three decimals in Arabic-Indic digits.

examples.title: Exact compact notation
examples.note: Rounded once from the exact amount: 999,999.995 is $1M, not $999.99K or $1.00M.

examples.title: ISO 4217 lookup
examples.note: Loaded on demand. Type a code or a numeric code.

keyboard: Not a UI module.
accessibility: Use `formatSpoken` for screen readers: it names the currency where a symbol is shared. Set `lang` on text printed in another script.
responsive: Compact notation where width is tight; full figures where the amount is agreed to.

notes.title: Where Intl and ISO differ
points: CLDR prints some currencies with fewer decimals than ISO 4217 because the coins are out of use: AFN, ALL, COP, HUF, IDR, IQD, IRR, KPW, LAK, LBP, MGA, MMK, PKR, RSD, SOS, SYP and YER. If your ledger stores ISO minor units, pass `exponent: isoMinorUnits(code)`.
CLDR groups en-PK and en-LK in thousands. Many Pakistani screens use lakh and crore; choose with `grouping`.

items.title: Payment fields
items.description: React inputs for IBAN, card number, expiry and CVC, SWIFT/BIC, IFSC, UPI ID, UK sort code, US routing and Nepal bank accounts: checked, grouped, paste-safe.
items.summary: Eleven inputs for the identifiers people type when they pay or get paid. Each accepts a paste with spaces, dashes or Devanagari and other scripts' digits, removes invisible characters (and says so), groups the text the way it is printed, keeps the caret in place, and sets the right `inputmode` and `autocomplete` (`cc-number`, `cc-exp`, `cc-csc` for cards). Problems are explained once the field is left; validity and what was detected (card network, IBAN country) are announced politely. The card number and security code are never written to a DOM attribute, even on the server, and a valid card number shows as "•••• 4242" when the field is not focused. `UpiInput` flags an address that looks like a saved payee's without being it, with the same check as `TransferReview`.
use: Payee and beneficiary forms: `IbanInput` with `BicInput` for international transfers, `SortCodeInput` with `UkAccountNumberInput`, `AbaRoutingInput`, `IfscInput`, `NepalBankAccountInput`.
Card forms you host yourself, inside your PCI DSS scope: `CardNumberInput` with `CardExpiryInput` and `CardCvcInput` (pass the detected `brand` so the code length follows it).
`UpiInput` with `knownPayees` set to the person's saved UPI IDs.
`NepalBankAccountInput` with a `rule` per bank, from your own bank list.
avoid: Treating a valid check as a verified account. It catches typing slips; the bank, the scheme or Confirmation of Payee says whether the account exists and whose it is.
Card fields outside your PCI scope: if your provider offers hosted fields, use them.
Logging `onValueChange` results for card fields.

notes.title: Security boundary
points: Card number and security code reach the input's `value` property only, never its attribute (CSS attribute selectors could read it), and are left out of server-rendered HTML. The components never log.
Nothing here stores, tokenises or sends card data. Your PCI DSS obligations are unchanged.
Nepal account rules are yours to supply: banks change formats, and the package ships no bank's format as fact.

items.title: Payment validation
items.description: Pure TypeScript checks for IBAN mod-97, card Luhn and brand by IIN range, expiry, SWIFT/BIC, IFSC, UPI, UK sort code, ABA routing and Nepal accounts.
items.summary: Pure functions with no React and no browser globals, so the same checks run in the browser and on your server. Every parser accepts pasted text (spaces, dashes, any script's digits, invisible characters removed) and returns `{ state, value, display, reason, cleaned }`: `state` is empty, partial, valid or invalid; `value` is the canonical text to store; `display` is the grouped text to show. IBANs are checked against the per-country structure from the SWIFT registry and mod-97; cards by IIN range, length and Luhn, with a masked form that never shows more than four digits; expiry against a `today` you can pass; ABA routing numbers by their weighted check digit. Brand and country tables are data you can replace.
use: Server-side validation of the same fields, with the same answers as the inputs.
`maskCardNumber` for receipts and saved-card lists.
`CARD_BRANDS` and `IBAN_FORMATS` extended with your own entries when a scheme changes, without waiting for a release.
avoid: Using a valid result as proof the account exists.
Checking card numbers outside your PCI DSS scope.

exports.name: parseIban
exports.description:
Check a typed or pasted IBAN: spaces, dashes, a leading "IBAN" and invisible characters are dropped, any script's
digits are read, and letters are uppercased. Never throws.

exports.name: formatIbanGroups
exports.description: "GB82WEST12345698765432" to "GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 32". Works on partial input; does not validate.

exports.name: ibanLength
exports.description: The IBAN length for a country from its BBAN structure, or null for a country without IBANs in the table.
exports.signature: (country: string, formats?: Readonly<Record<string, string>> | undefined) => number | null

exports.name: ibanCheckDigits
exports.description: Compute the two check digits for a country code and BBAN ("GB", "WEST12345698765432" gives "82").

exports.name: IBAN_FORMATS
exports.description:
BBAN structure per country, in the registry's notation without "!": digits (n), uppercase letters (a) and
alphanumerics (c), with lengths. The IBAN length is 4 plus the BBAN length. From the SWIFT IBAN registry
(checked 2026-11). Pass your own `formats` to add a country before a release.

exports.name: parseCardNumber
exports.description: Check a card number. Spaces, dashes and any script's digits are accepted. Never throws, never logs.

exports.name: detectCardBrand
exports.description: The brand of a (partial) card number by longest matching IIN prefix, or null. Needs the first digits only.
exports.signature: (input: string, brands?: readonly CardBrand[] | undefined) => CardBrand | null

exports.name: formatCardNumber
exports.description: "4242424242424242" to "4242 4242 4242 4242" with the brand's grouping (Amex 4-6-5). Works on partial input.
exports.signature: (input: string, brands?: readonly CardBrand[] | undefined) => string

exports.name: maskCardNumber
exports.description: The last four only, behind dots: "•••• 4242". Never more than four digits, and nothing for fewer than eight.

exports.name: parseCardExpiry
exports.description:
Check an expiry typed as MM/YY, MMYY, MM/YYYY or M/YY. A card is valid through the end of its expiry month. The
value is "MM/YY"; the display is "MM / YY" as printed on the card.

exports.name: parseCardCvc
exports.description: Check a security code: 3 digits, or 4 for a brand with `cvcLength: 4` (Amex). Without a brand, 3 or 4.
exports.signature: (input: string, brand?: CardBrand | null | undefined) => PaymentCheck

exports.name: CARD_BRANDS
exports.description:
Brands by IIN range, from the networks' published ranges (checked 2026-11). Where ranges overlap, the longest
matching prefix wins; on a tie the earlier entry wins. RuPay shares 65 with Discover and 353/356 with JCB through
network agreements, so those numbers report Discover or JCB. Pass your own table for local schemes.

exports.name: luhnValid
exports.description: The Luhn (mod 10) check on a string of ASCII digits. False for anything else or fewer than two digits.

exports.name: parseBic
exports.description: Check a SWIFT/BIC code: 8 or 11 characters, institution letters, a real country code, location and branch.

exports.name: isCountryCode
exports.description: True for an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (and XK).

exports.name: parseIfsc
exports.description: Check an Indian Financial System Code: four bank letters, a zero, then six branch characters (SBIN0001234).

exports.name: parseUpiVpa
exports.description:
Check a UPI Virtual Payment Address ("name@bank"). Case-insensitive, so the value is lowercase. A pasted
"upi://pay?pa=…" link is read for its address. Letters outside ASCII are refused, which also rules out look-alike
letters from other scripts.

exports.name: parseSortCode
exports.description: Check a UK sort code: six digits, shown as 12-34-56.

exports.name: parseUkAccountNumber
exports.description:
Check a UK account number: eight digits. A few banks issue six or seven; with `padShort` those are padded with
leading zeros, as Pay.UK's modulus-checking guidance describes. The sort-code-specific modulus check is not done here
(it needs Pay.UK's weight tables): use your provider's or Confirmation of Payee.
exports.signature: (input: string, options?: { padShort?: boolean | undefined; } | undefined) => PaymentCheck

exports.name: parseAbaRouting
exports.description:
Check a US ABA routing transit number: nine digits, a Federal Reserve prefix (00 to 12, 21 to 32, 61 to 72 or 80)
and the check digit.

exports.name: abaChecksumValid
exports.description: The ABA check: 3 × (d1 + d4 + d7) + 7 × (d2 + d5 + d8) + (d3 + d6 + d9) is a multiple of 10.

exports.name: parseNepalBankAccount
exports.description:
Check a Nepal bank account number against a bank's rule (`NEPAL_BANK_ACCOUNT_DEFAULT` when none is given).
Devanagari digits, spaces and dashes are accepted. A valid shape is not an existing account: confirm with the bank
(for example a name lookup through your payment switch) before you send money.

exports.name: NEPAL_BANK_ACCOUNT_DEFAULT
exports.description: The rule used when no bank is chosen: 8 to 20 digits, the range seen across Nepali banks.

exports.name: compactPaymentInput
exports.description:
Pasted or typed text to a compact ASCII form: digits of any supported script (Devanagari, Bengali, Arabic-Indic and
more) become ASCII, full-width letters become ASCII, spaces, dashes, dots and slashes are dropped, and invisible
characters are removed. Letters are uppercased unless `keepCase` is set. Other characters are kept, so a check can
refuse them.
exports.signature: (text: string, options?: { keepCase?: boolean | undefined; keepSeparators?: boolean | undefined; } | undefined) => { text: string; cleaned: boolean; }

exports.name: mod97
exports.description: ISO 7064 mod 97-10 remainder of an alphanumeric string (letters count as 10 to 35), without bigint.

exports.name: PaymentCheck
exports.description: The common result of every payment check.

notes.title: Limits
points: UK account numbers are not modulus-checked against the sort code (that needs Pay.UK's weight tables); use Confirmation of Payee.
RuPay shares IIN ranges with Discover (65) and JCB (353, 356), which report as Discover or JCB. UnionPay numbers are not Luhn-checked.
IFSC and UPI checks are shape only: there is no public check digit.

items.title: TaxInvoice
items.description: A printable Nepal VAT invoice: seller and buyer PAN, invoice number, BS and AD dates, lines, discount, exact 13% VAT, total and amount in words.
items.summary: A tax invoice as a document: the seller with logo, address and PAN/VAT number; the buyer and their PAN; the invoice number, the date in Bikram Sambat and Gregorian, a due date and the payment mode; the lines with quantity, unit, rate and amount; subtotal, discount, taxable and exempt amounts, VAT at the rate you pass (default 13%), the total, and the total in words (English or Nepali). Every figure comes from `computeInvoice` in exact bigint minor units, with a rounding mode you choose. It has its own print styles: plain background, no buttons, rows never split across pages.
use: The bill a shop, distributor or service firm hands over or emails: a VAT invoice, a quotation or a proforma (change `labels.title`).
A reprint with `copyMark` ("Copy of original (1)").
Compare `onTotals` with the totals your server stored before printing.
avoid: Treating it as the record. The invoice number, the VAT rate in force, what is exempt, cancellations and reporting to the tax authority are yours.
An editable bill: use LineItemEditor to build the lines, then show them here.

items.title: ReconciliationMatcher
items.description: Bank reconciliation in React: match statement lines to ledger entries one-to-one or many-to-one, accept exact suggestions, and see the reconciliation statement.
items.summary: A bank statement beside the bank account in the books. Tick lines on both sides and match them when their totals agree exactly (one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many, such as a payroll paid as five transfers), accept the exact-amount suggestions within a date window (`suggestMatches`), undo a match, and read the reconciliation statement: balance per bank plus deposits in transit less outstanding payments, against balance per books plus receipts and less charges the books do not have yet (`reconciliationSummary`). Amounts are signed bigint minor units from the account holder's side, so money in is positive on both lists. It is controlled: you keep the matches. `onCreateEntry` puts a "Book" action on statement-only lines so you can post them.
use: Month-end bank reconciliation in an accounting app; card, wallet or payment-gateway settlement against the books.
Keep `matches` on your server with the statement, so a reconciliation can be reopened and audited.
avoid: Deciding what a bank error is or posting journals itself: it reports the difference and offers the action; your books do the posting.
Very long statements (thousands of lines) in one go: filter by date or amount first.

props.name: statement
props.description: Lines from the bank statement, signed: money in positive, money out negative.

props.name: ledger
props.description: Entries posted to the bank account in the books, signed the same way.

props.name: matches
props.description: The matches made so far (controlled).

props.name: onMatchesChange
props.description: Called with the next matches after a match, an accepted suggestion or an undo.

props.name: statementBalance
props.description: Closing balance on the statement. With `ledgerBalance`, shows the reconciliation statement.

props.name: ledgerBalance
props.description: Closing balance of the account in the books on the same date.

props.name: onCreateEntry
props.description: Offer a "Book" action on an unmatched statement line (bank charges, interest), so the host can post it.

props.name: dateWindow
props.description: Most days between dates for a suggestion. Default 5.

props.name: newMatchId
props.type: ((statementIds: readonly string[], ledgerIds: readonly string[]) => string)
props.description: Makes a fresh id for a manual match. Default: `m-` and the first statement id.

props.name: money
props.description: Currency and locale. Default NPR, en-IN grouping, no currency mark.

props.description: How a date is written. Default `formatCalendarDate`.

props.name: headingLevel
props.description: Heading level of the panel, matched and summary headings. Default 3.

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Height of each list before it scrolls (the list is then a focusable region). Default 360.

props.name: labels
props.description: Words, in the reader's language.

props.description: Called when the retry button is pressed.

props.name: testId
props.description: Sets `data-testid` on the root; parts get `${testId}-match`, `-auto`, `-difference`, `-s-<id>`, `-l-<id>` and so on.

exports.name: suggestMatches
exports.description:
One-to-one suggestions: the same exact amount within the date window. Equal references come first, then the
nearest date, then input order; each item is used once. Suggestions only: show them and let a person confirm.
exports.signature: (statement: readonly ReconcileItem[], ledger: readonly ReconcileItem[], options?: SuggestOptions | undefined) => ReconcileMatch[]

exports.name: reconciliationSummary

exports.name: matchDifference
exports.description: Statement total minus ledger total of a match; zero when the match balances. Unknown ids throw.
exports.signature: (statement: readonly ReconcileItem[], ledger: readonly ReconcileItem[], match: Pick<ReconcileMatch, "ledgerIds" | "statementIds">) => bigint

exports.name: sumAmounts
exports.description: Exact sum of the amounts of the items given.

props.description: Unique and stable within its side (statement or ledger).

props.name: date

props.name: amount

props.description: Unique and stable: a key for the row.

props.name: statementIds
props.description: Statement line ids in this match (one or more).

props.name: ledgerIds
props.description: Ledger entry ids in this match (one or more).

props.name: unmatchedStatement
props.description: Statement lines in no match: interest, charges and receipts the books have not recorded yet.

props.name: unmatchedLedger
props.description: Ledger entries in no match: deposits in transit and payments the bank has not cleared yet.

props.name: depositsInTransit
props.description: Ledger-only money in (deposits in transit).

props.description: Ledger-only money out, as a positive amount (outstanding cheques and payments).

props.description: Statement-only money out, as a positive amount, not yet in the books.

props.name: reconciled
props.description: difference is zero and every match balances.

items.title: Invest helpers
items.description: Pure exact mutual fund maths: XIRR by bisection on bigint fixed point, SIP and step-up projections, the SIP for a goal, units at a NAV and life cover needed.
items.summary: Pure functions in @punji/ui/invest. `xirr(flows)` solves the annual rate of dated cash flows (actual/365) by bisection with 36-place bigint fixed point, rounded half-even to 8 places, and `xnpv` checks it. `projectSip` grows monthly instalments (with an optional yearly step-up rounded to whole rupees) at an expected return compounded monthly, carrying the balance as an exact fraction and rounding each reported figure once; `projectLumpSum` does the same for one payment, and `sipForGoal` finds the smallest instalment that reaches a goal. `allotUnits` and `unitsValue` convert between money and units at a decimal NAV, rounding units down so the cost never exceeds the payment. `termCoverNeeded` is the income-replacement cover gap. Amounts are bigint minor units; no React, no browser globals.
use: Fund statements, SIP calculators and goal planners that must agree with the server to the paisa.
Portfolio XIRR from every dated instalment and today's value.
avoid: Tax on gains, exit loads and stamp duty: apply them around these.
Promising returns: a projection is an illustration at the rate you pass.

exports.name: xirr
exports.description: The XIRR of dated cash flows, or null when they have no rate (all one sign, or no root in range).
exports.signature: (flows: readonly CashFlow[], options?: XirrOptions | undefined) => XirrResult | null

exports.name: xnpv
exports.description:
The net present value of the flows at an annual rate (a decimal fraction string, '0.12' for 12%), discounted to
the first flow's date, in minor units rounded with `rounding` (default half-even). At the XIRR it is zero to within
the rounding of the rate.
exports.signature: (flows: readonly CashFlow[], rate: string, rounding?: "ceil" | "floor" | "half-even" | "half-up" | "trunc" | undefined) => bigint

exports.name: projectSip
exports.description: Project a monthly SIP with an optional yearly step-up.
exports.signature: ({ monthly, months, annualReturnPercent, stepUpPercent, stepUpEvery, roundTo, rounding }: SipInput) => SipProjection

exports.name: projectLumpSum
exports.description: A one-time investment grown at the same monthly-compounded rate as `projectSip`, rounded once.
exports.signature: ({ amount, months, annualReturnPercent, rounding }: LumpSumInput) => { invested: bigint; value: bigint; gain: bigint; }

exports.name: sipForGoal
exports.description:
The smallest first instalment, a multiple of `roundTo`, whose projection reaches `goal`. Starts from the exact
no-step-up answer and checks with `projectSip`, so the answer agrees with the projection shown next to it.

exports.name: allotUnits
exports.description: Units for an amount at a NAV. Rounding defaults to 'floor'.
exports.signature: (amount: bigint, nav: string | Nav, { unitDecimals, exponent, rounding }?: (UnitOptions & { rounding?: RoundingMode | undefined; }) | undefined) => Allotment

exports.name: unitsValue
exports.description: The value of units at a NAV in minor units. Rounding defaults to 'half-even'.
exports.signature: (units: bigint, nav: string | Nav, { unitDecimals, exponent, rounding }?: (UnitOptions & { rounding?: RoundingMode | undefined; }) | undefined) => bigint

exports.name: parseNav
exports.description: Parse a positive NAV per unit ('10.4567'): up to 9 integer and 8 fraction digits.

exports.name: formatUnits
exports.description: Units as a decimal string.

exports.name: termCoverNeeded
exports.description: Life cover still needed.
exports.signature: ({ annualIncome, years, incomeSharePercent, liabilities, goals, savings, existingCover, roundTo }: CoverInput) => CoverResult

examples.title: XIRR, SIP, units, cover
examples.note: The Excel XIRR example gives 37.336253%; Rs 5,000 a month at 12% for 10 years is Rs 11,61,695.38.

keyboard: Not interactive.
accessibility: Not applicable: pure functions.
responsive: Not applicable: pure functions.

notes.title: Precision
points: XIRR: bisection until the bracket is narrower than 10^-(digits+2), then half-even to `digits` places (default 8): within one unit in the last place of the true root. Flows with no sign change return null; with several sign changes, a root in the first bracket where the value changes sign (searching up from -99.9999%).
SIP and lump sum: no intermediate rounding; tested against the closed form and with fast-check (XIRR of a SIP puts its NPV at zero; units never cost more than the payment).

items.title: Trading terminal
items.description: A complete NEPSE trading terminal built from Punji UI: live market watch, candles, depth and order book, an order ticket that fills orders, positions and P&L.
items.summary: A trading terminal of the kind a NEPSE broker's TMS offers, running on a simulated session. Quotes tick every 1.5 seconds; an order you place on the ticket goes into the order book, fills in lots when the market reaches your limit, pays exact NEPSE fees, moves your cash and changes your position. Every screen reads one account state, so the cash on Positions, the buying power on the ticket and the fills in the trade book agree to the paisa.
use: Replace `site/src/apps/shared/sim.ts` with your broker's feed: the screens read `Quote` objects with bigint paisa, the same shape `StockTable` takes.
Send `onSubmit` from `OrderTicket` to your order API instead of the reducer; map your order statuses to `TradingOrder`.
Keep the fee schedule current: `estimateNepseTrade` reads `nepseFeeSchedule`, an example to verify against SEBON notices.
avoid: Authentication, the broker connection, collateral rules and risk checks: the reducer only checks buying power and holdings.
Order types beyond a day limit order (stop, IOC) and the exchange's own matching: fills here are a seeded simulation.
keyboard: `1` to `5` open the screens; `B` and `S` open the ticket on the selected scrip as a buy or a sell; `P` pauses and resumes the live prices.
`/`, `Ctrl+K` or `⌘K` (and `?`) open the command palette: type a symbol, a screen or a command; Left and Right choose between a scrip's actions (Chart, Buy, Sell, Watch); Enter runs it, Esc closes.
Plain keys never fire while you type in a field. The order ticket steps quantity in lots and price in ticks with the arrow keys; the split pane's separator moves with the arrow keys, Home and End.
accessibility: Each screen has its own `h2`; opening one from the navigation moves focus to it. The navigation marks the current screen with `aria-current`.
Fills, rejections and cancellations are announced in a polite live region; a circuit-breaker halt is an alert. Direction is never colour alone: signs, arrows and words.
Live prices honour reduced motion (no count-up or flash) and can be paused.
responsive: Wide screens: a navigation rail, the quote table beside the selected scrip, and the chart and ticket in a resizable split pane.
Phones and tablets: a bottom tab bar, tables become stacked rows, and the split pane stacks the chart above the ticket.

notes.title: Limits
points: Synthetic scrips and prices; the session starts at 12:00 on 1 November 2026 and five simulated seconds pass per tick.
Capital gains tax on a sell uses the long-term rate for positions carried from earlier sessions and the short-term rate for today's buys.
The circuit breaker is a demo control (Commands, "Trip the index circuit breaker"): it marks every scrip down about 4.3% and pauses trading for 15 simulated minutes.

items.title: Wealth dashboard

Tax lots, multi-currency assets and liabilities: net worth here is shares, savings, money blocked for applications and fixed deposits.

items.title: Accounting
items.description: A double-entry accounting app built from Punji UI: ledger, journals, trial balance, P&L and balance sheet by BS fiscal year, bank reconciliation, aging and TDS.

items.title: Retail banking
items.description: A mobile-first retail banking app built from Punji UI: balances, statements in BS and AD, a transfer with payee check and OTP, cards, loans, deposits and KYC.
items.summary: A retail bank's app, phone first, on a simulated customer. Three accounts with three months of statements; a transfer that checks the payee's name with the receiving bank, says the amount in words, asks for a one-time code and prints a receipt; cards you can freeze, limit, block and replace; a home loan with its exact schedule and an early EMI; fixed deposits; a KYC update with the Nepal address picker and document upload; and notifications. One reducer holds the money, so the balance on Home, the statement's running balance, the receipt and the notification agree to the paisa.
use: Replace the reducer's actions with your core banking API: `transfer`, `card-status`, `pay-emi`, `open-fd` and `kyc-submit` are the calls a bank makes; keep the screens.
Feed `PayeeVerification` the answer from your Confirmation of Payee or ConnectIPS name lookup, and record the acknowledgement with the payment.
Send the OTP from your server and check it there; the demo accepts 246810 so the flow can be tried.
avoid: Authentication, device binding, session timeouts and fraud scoring: the app starts signed in.
The fee schedule and limits: ConnectIPS-style fees and a Rs 10 lakh daily limit are illustrations, not any bank's tariff.
keyboard: `1` to `7` open the screens; `H` hides and shows balances.
The payee picker is a combobox (arrows, Enter, Escape); the code boxes take digits, Backspace and paste; segmented controls move with the arrow keys.
Every money action has a confirm step you reach with Tab and Enter: Review, then the code, for a transfer; an inline confirm to unfreeze or block a card, pay an EMI or open a deposit.
accessibility: Each screen has its own `h2` and focus moves to it from the navigation; each transfer step moves focus to its heading. What the app did is announced in a polite live region.
Account and card numbers are masked and spoken as "ending in"; "Hide balances" replaces every figure with dots and the word hidden.
The payee check is a live region; statuses are words and icons, never colour alone.
responsive: Designed at 390 px: quick actions in a 3 by 2 grid, stacked cards and a bottom tab bar. Tablets and desktops get a navigation rail and two columns.
Print or Save as PDF from the statement drops the app chrome and prints every entry.

notes.title: Limits
points: Punji Bank and every name, number and balance are invented. The session is 1 November 2026 (15 Kartik 2083), 10:30 Kathmandu time.
"Offline (demo)" makes the bank unreachable: statements fail with a retry and nothing that moves money goes through.
The OTP is shown on screen for the demo. A real bank never shows it, and limits tries on its server.

items.title: Digital wallet
items.description: An eSewa and Khalti class digital wallet built from Punji UI: balance and load money, scan and pay EMVCo QR, send to mobile with a PIN, bills, top-up, rewards.
items.summary: A digital wallet of the eSewa and Khalti kind, phone first. Load money from a linked bank; scan a merchant's NepalPay-style QR (paste a payload or pick a sample) and see the merchant and amount the code carries before you pay; send money to a mobile number; pay electricity, water and internet bills and top up a phone; follow every payment's timeline; and earn and redeem cashback. Every payment is confirmed with a `PinPad` whose digits are never written to the page. One reducer holds the balance, so Home, History, the receipt and Rewards agree to the paisa.
use: Swap the reducer's actions for your wallet API: `load`, `pay` and `redeem`; each payment carries the PIN for your server to check.
Decode the camera's QR text and pass it to `parseMerchantQr`; the screen already handles static and dynamic codes and every parse error.
Replace the simulated billers in `bills.ts` with your biller gateway: the screen needs a lookup that returns the lines for a `BillSummary`.
avoid: Checking the PIN in the browser: the demo compares it with 2580 so the flow can be tried; your server must check it and count attempts.
The limits and cashback rules: they are illustrations, not Nepal Rastra Bank's or any wallet's.
keyboard: `1` to `6` open the screens; `H` hides and shows the balance.
The PIN pad and the amount keypad take digit keys and Backspace while focused, and arrow keys move between their keys.
Sample QR codes, billers and plans are buttons and segmented controls: Tab, arrows, Enter and Space.
accessibility: Each screen has its own `h2`; focus moves to it from the navigation and to each step's heading inside a flow. Payments are announced in a polite live region.
The PIN pad announces "2 of 4 digits entered" and nothing else; a wrong PIN is an alert.
Statuses are words and icon shapes; amounts carry their sign and direction in words.
responsive: Designed at 390 px with a bottom tab bar; wider screens get a navigation rail and the flow beside its summary.
The payment detail opens in a sheet that fits the phone.

notes.title: Limits
points: Every merchant, biller, person and number is invented. The session is 1 November 2026, 10:30 Kathmandu time.
The demo PIN is 2580; three wrong PINs lock payments for the session. Sending to 9841000000 is refused as not registered.
A load from the bank settles a few seconds later, and one pending internet payment fails and is refunded, so the timeline shows each outcome.

items.title: Market portal
items.description: A public NEPSE market portal built from Punji UI: indices, breadth, sector heatmap, a screener, a 10k-trade floorsheet, company pages, calendars and alerts.
items.summary: The public side of the market: what a reader of a market data site sees before they trade. Ninety-six listed companies tick live; every trade is written to the floorsheet with its buying and selling broker, and each company's volume and turnover are those contracts summed, so the floorsheet, the overview, the screener and the company page agree to the paisa. Valuation ratios use the live price over trailing EPS and book value, the sector heatmap is sized by the same turnover, the calendars list the same book closures and AGMs the company pages show, and price alerts fire on the tick the price crosses.
use: Replace `site/src/apps/market-portal/market.ts` with your data feed: the screens read `LiveQuote` objects (bigint paisa, the `Quote` shape `StockTable` takes) and `FloorTrade` contracts.
Feed fundamentals (EPS, book value, dividends) from published reports; `fundamentalsOf` recomputes P/E, P/B, yield and market cap from the live price.
Keep watchlists and alerts on your server per reader and send the alert from there; the reducer only shows how they fire against the ticks.
avoid: Real prices, published financials and corporate announcements: everything here is generated. Verify against NEPSE, SEBON and company notices.
Trading: the portal links to nothing that places orders. The trading terminal app shows that side.
keyboard: `1` to `7` open the screens; `P` pauses and resumes the live prices. Plain keys never fire while you type in a field.

The screener and floorsheet tables move between rows with the arrow keys; Enter on a column head sorts it and Shift+Enter adds it to the sort. Filter chips open their editor; Esc closes it and returns focus to the chip.
Company search fields take the arrow keys and Enter; the watchlist moves a symbol up or down with its buttons.
accessibility: Each screen has its own `h2` and focus moves to it from the navigation. Alerts that fire, watchlist changes and the feed dropping are announced in a polite live region.
Direction is never colour alone: arrows, signs and words, and breadth counts in text. The heatmap, charts and depth have their figures in tables.
Scrolling tables and chip rows are focusable regions; live prices honour reduced motion and can be paused.
responsive: Wide screens: a navigation rail, index cards, the heatmap beside the movers and the company page in two columns.
Phones (390 px first): a bottom tab bar, the indices as a scrolling strip, a square heatmap, and tables that scroll inside their own focusable region with the symbol pinned.

notes.title: Limits
points: Synthetic companies, prices, results and events. The session is 1 November 2026, opening at 11:00 and closing at 15:00; the page opens at 11:20 after twenty minutes of trading, and each tick is five simulated seconds.
The floorsheet starts with about 13,000 contracts and grows while the market is open. Broker numbers are random.
Dividends are shown on 100 shares with bonus shares at par; the company page's results are derived from the trailing EPS.

items.title: Invest and insure
items.description: A mutual fund and insurance app built from Punji UI: fund explorer with riskometers, SIP planner and orders, portfolio XIRR, policies, claims and tax saving.
items.summary: An investor's app for mutual funds and insurance, phone first. Explore eight funds by category with a riskometer, 1, 3 and 5-year returns, the expense ratio and the NAV history; plan a SIP with a step-up and a goal and see the exact projection against a lump sum; order it, follow the order to an allotment of units at NAV, and see the units, value and XIRR in the portfolio. On the insurance side: policy cards with premiums and due reminders, a term-cover gap from income and loans, claim filing with documents and a status timeline, and nominees whose shares must total 100%. The tax view adds up what reduces taxable income (retirement fund SIPs and CIT, life and health premiums) against example caps. One reducer holds the folio and the policies, so an allotment moves the portfolio, the savings in the cover gap and the retirement contribution in the tax view together.
use: Replace `data.ts` with your fund house's or aggregator's feed: the screens read NAVs as decimal strings and amounts as bigint paisa, the shape `allotUnits` and `unitsValue` take.
Send `order` to your order API (ConnectIPS or a bank mandate for the debit) and map its statuses to the order timeline; allot with the NAV the registrar applied, not the latest one.
Feed policies, premiums and claim statuses from the insurer's API; keep `termCoverNeeded` for the gap and `taxableIncome` with the caps for the year you show.
avoid: Authentication, KYC, the bank mandate and the registrar: orders here settle on a timer.
Advice: projections are illustrations at a return you choose, the cover gap is a starting point and the tax caps are examples, not current law.
keyboard: `1` to `5` open the screens. Plain keys never fire while you type in a field.
Funds are buttons (Enter opens one; "All funds" returns focus to it); categories are toggle chips; period, view and calendar switches are segmented controls that move with the arrow keys.
Order, claim and nominee forms are ordinary forms: Tab, Space and Enter; each step moves focus to its heading. Wide tables scroll in focusable regions with the arrow keys.
accessibility: Each screen has its own `h2` and focus moves to it from the navigation. Orders, allotments, premiums, claims and nominee changes are announced in a polite live region.
Risk is printed in words beside the riskometer ("Moderately high, 4 of 6"); returns and gains carry a sign, never colour alone; the NAV chart has a data table.
Statuses (order steps, claim steps, policy status, SIP paused) are words with icons.
responsive: Designed at 390 px: fund cards in one column, stacked forms and a bottom tab bar. Wider screens get a navigation rail, fund cards in a grid and the projection beside the plan.
Tables become labelled rows on phones; the SIP calendar scrolls inside a focusable region.

notes.title: Limits
points: Every fund house, insurer, fund and person is invented. NAVs are a seeded weekly series to 1 November 2026 (15 Kartik 2083); orders allot at that NAV.

Projections compound the expected return monthly with each instalment at the start of the month; the balance is carried exactly and each figure is rounded once (half-even). XIRR is solved by bisection on bigint fixed-point to 0.01% here (8 places in the package).

Tax caps and slabs are examples in the shape of FY 2081/82 (retirement 5 lakh or a third of income, life premium Rs 40,000, health premium Rs 20,000). "Fail the next request" makes orders, premiums and claims fail so the error states can be seen.
